# 4.2 Example 1

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

Let's consider the following passage. Does it contain an argument? Is it
trying to convince us of something, or establish that something is true?

> "Contrary to popular opinion, cultural relativism is not simply the thesis
> that different cultures have different views about what's right and
> wrong. Instead, cultural relativism advances the much stronger claim
> that there is nothing *more* to morality than these different views
> and that there is no objective, culturally-transcendent right and
> wrong in the ethical realm. According to cultural relativism, every
> culture determines what's right and wrong for itself."

It doesn't look to me like this passage is trying to convince us of
anything, so I'd say that it doesn't contain an argument. It's simply
telling us what the philosophical position of cultural relativism is.

## Summary of Example 1

Example 1 presented us with the following passage:

> "Contrary to popular opinion, cultural relativism is not simply the thesis
> that different cultures have different views about what's right and
> wrong. Instead, cultural relativism advances the much stronger claim
> that there is nothing *more* to morality than these different views
> and that there is no objective, culturally-transcendent right and
> wrong in the ethical realm. According to cultural relativism, every
> culture determines what's right and wrong for itself."

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We decided that this passage doesn't contain an argument.
